summary: What the evidence supports: Taiwan's idle-test limits are lenient. A pre-2004 scooter may legally idle at 4.5% CO and 9000 ppm HC, a 2004-2007 build at 3.5% and 1600-2000 ppm, a 2017-or-later build at 2.0% and 1000 ppm (gazette, verified). Inspection covers only scooters 5+ years old, at idle only: in 2025, 8.18 million four-strokes were tested (82.84% attendance, 3.78% failed); old two-strokes 44.04% attendance, 8.39% failed; failure is about 5.1-5.6% at ages 17+. Lab tests show newer phases emit about half the CO and HC per km of Phase III, with NOx not improved; a three-scooter Taichung case study found a deteriorated Phase IV scooter at 14x the CO and 32x the HC of a Phase VII one. Cold start raises CO up to about 1.5x and HC up to about 2.8x. Idle-stop is mandated by engine-family share, and its tailpipe benefit is unproven. The record does not support: idling emitting more particles than driving, scooters out-emitting cars on PM2.5 or NOx, a measured pull-away spike, or a high-emitter fleet share. The honest pedestrian-facing story is CO, hydrocarbons and benzene concentrated at an intersection; the health effects need separate evidence.

findings.claim: Taiwan's in-use motorcycle idle-test limits (CO %, HC ppm) are 4.5% / 9000 ppm for scooters built before 2004, 3.5% / 2000 ppm for 2004 builds, 3.5% / 1600 ppm from July 2007, and 2.0% / 1000 ppm from 2017 (unchanged for the 2021 phase 7).
findings.value: In-use (periodic inspection) idle limits, motorcycles <700 cc: 1980-2003 standards: CO 4.5%, HC 9000 ppm (opacity 30% from the 1988 rows on); built from 1 Jan 2004: CO 3.5%, HC 2000 ppm; from 1 Jul 2007: CO 3.5%, HC 1600 ppm; from 1 Jan 2017 and from 1 Jan 2021: CO 2.0%, HC 1000 ppm. 700 cc and above stay on the 2002 standard (4.5% / 9000 ppm). 2.0% CO = 20,000 ppm.
findings.setting: Taiwan; in-use idle-state test; limits apply by manufacture date. Gazette text 30 June 2023.
findings.citation: Ministry of Environment (Taiwan) / Executive Yuan Gazette vol. 29 no. 121 (30 June 2023), Standards for Air Pollutant Emissions from Mobile Sources (移動污染源空氣污染物排放標準), Article 6 table.
findings.design: Primary legal text. Verifier downloaded the gazette PDF, ran pdftotext -layout and read the Article 6 rows labelled 使用中車輛檢驗 beside each effective date.
findings.quote: 中華民國九十三年一月一日 ... 使用中車輛檢驗 － 3.5 2000 30 30; 九十六年七月一日 ... － 3.5 1600 30 30; 一百零六年一月一日 ... － 2.0 1000 30 30; 一百十年一月一日 ... － 2.0 1000 30 30; 七十七/八十/八十七/九十一年 rows: － 4.5 9000 30 30
findings.caveats: Pass/fail limit, not typical emission: a passing 2017-or-later scooter may still idle at 2.0% CO and 1000 ppm HC. Limits for NEW vehicles at type approval are a little stricter than the in-use limits (e.g. 3.0% CO / 2000 ppm for 2004, 3.0% / 1600 ppm for 2007). The 1980 row has 4.5% / 9000 ppm without an opacity limit. The row-to-date mapping is now confirmed from the layout-preserved text, not just reading order.
findings.useOnSite: A scooter built before 2004 is legally allowed 4.5% CO and 9000 ppm HC at idle; one built from 2017 is allowed 2.0% and 1000 ppm: permitted idle CO is cut by 56% and permitted idle HC by a factor of nine.
findings.verifierNote: Re-read the gazette PDF independently; every limit and effective date in the claim matches. Added the 700 cc+ and new-vehicle-vs-in-use nuances.

findings.claim: Taiwan's driving-cycle limits for new scooters (<700 cc) fell from 7.3-8.8 g/km CO and 4.4-5.5 g/km HC+NOx (1988) to 1.0 g/km CO and 0.1 g/km THC (2021), but the test procedure changed along the way (CO went UP on paper in 2004), so only adjacent standards of the same procedure are comparable.
findings.value: New-type limits, g/km, <700 cc (CO | HC+NOx; prototype/production unless stated): pre-1988 10.2 | 6.5; 1 Jan 1988 7.3/8.8 | 4.4/5.5; 1 Jul 1991 3.75/4.5 | 2.4/3.0; 1 Jan 1998 3.25/3.5 | 1.75/2.0 (same for 2002 <700 cc); 1 Jan 2004 7.0 | 2.0 four-stroke, 1.0 two-stroke (new test procedure); 1 Jul 2007 (<150 cc) CO 2.0, HC 0.8, NOx 0.15 g/km (>=150 cc HC 0.3); 1 Jan 2017 (<130 km/h) CO 1140, HC 380, NOx 70 mg/km, OBD required (>=130 km/h: 1140/170/90); 1 Jan 2021 CO 1000, THC 100, NMHC 68, NOx 60, PM 4.5 mg/km (PM only for direct-injection engines).
findings.setting: Taiwan; new-type approval and new-vehicle inspection, chassis-dynamometer cycle (CNS 11386 to 2003; Taiwan motorcycle procedure 2004-2016; WMTC-based from 2017 per ARTC).
findings.citation: Ministry of Environment (Taiwan) / Executive Yuan Gazette vol. 29 no. 121 (30 June 2023), Standards for Air Pollutant Emissions from Mobile Sources (移動污染源空氣污染物排放標準), Article 6 table; ARTC article https://www.artc.org.tw/tw/knowledge/articles/2617 for phase/cycle context.
findings.design: Primary legal text read by the verifier from the gazette PDF (layout-preserved).
findings.caveats: ORIGINAL ERROR FIXED: in the pre-2007 rows the value after the g/km CO is HC+NOx, and the next number (4.5, 3.75/4.0, 3.0) is the new-vehicle idle CO %, not a g/km figure. HC+NOx therefore fell 4.4/5.5 -> 2.4/3.0 -> 1.75/2.0, not '3.75-4.5'. The 2004 CO of 7.0 g/km is not a loosening: the test procedure changed (ECE-type cycle, cold start); ARTC says the cycle changed again to WMTC from 2017. HC+NOx for four-strokes was 2.0 g/km in both 1998 and 2004. These are type-approval limits for new vehicles, not in-use emissions.
findings.useOnSite: Within comparable procedures: the 2007 (Euro 3-equivalent) standard allowed 2.0 g/km CO and 0.8 g/km HC (<150 cc); the 2021 standard allows 1.0 g/km CO and 0.1 g/km THC, with the cycle changed from ECE-type to WMTC. Do not quote 7.0 vs 1.0 g/km as a seven-fold improvement.
findings.verifierNote: HC+NOx and idle-CO columns were misread in the original (e.g. '1988 HC+NOx 4.5' is really 4.4/5.5 with 4.5 being the idle CO %; '1998 NOx 1.75/2.0, HC+NOx 3.75/4.0' is really HC+NOx 1.75/2.0 and idle CO 3.75/4.0 %; '2004 NOx 2.0, HC+NOx 3.0' is really HC+NOx 2.0 (four-stroke)/1.0 (two-stroke), 3.0 = idle CO %). CO, 2007, 2017 and 2021 values were right. The 'seven times' useOnSite comparison is withdrawn because of the cycle change.

findings.claim: In 2025, 8.18 million four-stroke scooters were inspected (82.84% of those notified) with a 3.78% failure rate, while pre-2004 two-stroke scooters had a 44.04% attendance rate and an 8.39% failure rate.
findings.setting: Taiwan nationwide periodic idle test of motorcycles 5+ years old; MOENV motorcycle inspection information system annual tables.
findings.citation: Ministry of Environment (Taiwan), 機車定期檢驗資訊管理系統, 歷年各行程別到檢率 and 不合格率 tables, Year 2024/12 and 2025/12.
findings.design: Verifier fetched both the attendance (year_Cycle_list.aspx) and failure (year_Cycle_list_NotOK.aspx) tables for 2024/12 and 2025/12 and read the 全國 rows.
findings.caveats: Table note 1: denominator not adjusted for scooters no longer in use, so attendance is understated. Failure rate is among inspected scooters only; non-attenders are probably dirtier. The two-stroke category is '93年以前出廠' i.e. built in ROC year 93 (2004) or earlier. Only 5+ year-old scooters are tested, at idle only.
findings.useOnSite: About 96 in 100 inspected four-stroke scooters pass the idle test; only about 44 in 100 of the oldest two-stroke scooters turn up and 8% of those fail.
findings.verifierNote: All numbers match the government tables.

findings.claim: Among inspected scooters, the idle-test failure rate is about 5.1-5.6% at ages 17 and above, versus about 2.4-3.5% at ages 10-15 (8.29 million inspections in 2025).
findings.setting: Taiwan, motorcycles aged 5+ years, idle test, 1 Jan-31 Dec 2025 (tabulated 3 Jan 2026), by age from manufacture date.
findings.citation: Ministry of Environment (Taiwan), 機車排氣定檢機車車齡不合格率統計表, 114.01.01-114.12.31.
findings.design: Verifier fetched the 2025/12 and 2024/12 tables and read every row.
findings.caveats: Age 16 is only 3.57%, so the step up starts at 17. Age 9 (4.53%) is a local peak. Non-monotonic because limits differ by build date and survivors differ. 'Other' (new/unknown age) 7.51% of 5,443. Non-attenders untested.
findings.useOnSite: Among inspected scooters 17 years or older, about 5 in 100 fail even the lenient idle test; the rate for scooters that skip inspection is unknown.
findings.verifierNote: Original said '16 years and above (about 5-6%)'; age 16 is 3.57%. Corrected to 17+ (5.10-5.63%).

findings.claim: A UDN report citing the EPA says that in 2021 attendance was about 76% nationally, about 60% for scooters 20+ years old, and the highest failure rate (6.25%) was among 20+ year-old scooters; only 3.65% of non-attenders were fined.
findings.value: 2021: 9.53 million scooters 5+ years old due, 7.27 million tested (about 76%); age <=7 y about 86%; >13 y mostly below 75%; 20+ y about 60%; 20+ y failure 6.25%; 82,414 fined = 3.65% of the roughly 2.25 million non-attenders.
findings.setting: Taiwan 2021 (ROC 110), as reported by UDN in 2022.
findings.citation: UDN 發燒車訊, '你驗排氣了嗎？全台225萬輛機車未排氣定檢 地方政府告發率僅3.65%'.
findings.design: Verifier opened the article and found each figure, attributed to the EPA.
findings.quote: 環保署統計，110年全台有953萬輛出廠五年以上的機車，依法必須接受空氣汙染物定期檢驗，但僅727萬輛機車有做檢測，到檢率約七成六
findings.caveats: Newspaper report, not primary data. The EPA official in the article attributes the 2021 dip to COVID-19 level-3 alert extensions. Attendance has since risen to about 83% (MOENV 2025 table).
findings.useOnSite: Enforcement is thin: in 2021 fewer than 4 in 100 non-attending scooters were fined (as reported by UDN from EPA data).
findings.verifierNote: All figures present in the article; COVID explanation confirmed in the article text.

findings.claim: In a Taiwanese chassis-dynamometer test of 40 four-stroke scooters, Phase V scooters emitted about 58% less CO and 43% less HC than Phase III, and exhaust worsened with age and mileage; NOx did not improve.
findings.value: Emission-factor ratios: Phase IV/III 0.66 (CO), 0.61 (HC); Phase V/III 0.42 (CO), 0.57 (HC). NOx order Phase V > IV > III. Total VOC Phase V 0.59 g/km (lowest). BTEX down 37-58% (IV) and 44-62% (V) vs Phase III.
findings.setting: Taiwan; 40 in-use four-stroke motorcycles, Phases III/IV/V, chassis dynamometer, ECE cycle, 52 VOCs.
findings.citation: Tsai J-H, Yao Y-C, Huang P-H, Chiang H-L (2017). Criteria Pollutants and Volatile Organic Compounds Emitted from Motorcycle Exhaust under Various Regulation Phases. Aerosol and Air Quality Research 17(5): 1214-1223.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex; authors, volume, pages via Crossref.
findings.quote: their ratios of emission factor of Phase IV to Phase III and Phase V to Phase III were 0.66 and 0.42 for CO and 0.61 and 0.57 for HC, respectively
findings.caveats: ECE cycle includes idle segments but idle is not reported separately. Only 40 vehicles. Age, mileage and phase are confounded. Abstract only.
findings.useOnSite: Taiwanese lab tests show Phase V scooters emit roughly half the CO and HC per km of Phase III scooters; NOx did not improve.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers confirmed. Citation corrected: Crossref lists four authors (Chiang H-L was omitted).

findings.claim: A Taichung real-world case study of three scooters found Phase IV scooters emitting 14.0 times the CO and 32.1 times the HC of Phase VII, with deteriorated Phase IV high-emitters at 6.36-6.94% CO; the authors conclude emissions were governed mainly by engine technology and maintenance, not driving pattern.
findings.value: Phase IV/VII ratios: 14.0 (CO), 32.1 (HC); IV-H high-emitters CO 6.36-6.94%, fuel up to 0.138 L/km; total VOC 22-28x; OFP 22-52x; idle share of the driving cycle lower in 2025 than in 2014.
findings.setting: Taichung, Taiwan; on-road driving data and real-world emission measurements, 2014 and 2025; three targeted motorcycles.
findings.citation: Tsai J-H, How V, He Z-J, Chan Y-C, Chiang H-L (2026). Characteristics of driving pattern and motorcycle emissions during the transition of urban transportation system: A case study of Taichung in Taiwan. Results in Engineering 32: 112353.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex; bibliographic data via Crossref (issue date shown as 2026-12).
findings.quote: Phase IV motorcycles (older generation) exhibited substantially higher emissions than Phase VII models (newer generation), with Phase IV/Phase VII emission ratios reaching 14.0 for CO and 32.1 for HC.
findings.caveats: Three vehicles: case-study ratios, not fleet averages. The split of the three vehicles (one Phase VII, two Phase IV) is not stated in the abstract. CO % is exhaust concentration under real-world driving, not specifically at idle.
findings.useOnSite: In a three-scooter Taichung case study a deteriorated older scooter emitted tens of times more hydrocarbons than a current-generation one; the authors say technology and maintenance mattered more than driving pattern. Not a fleet average.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers match the abstract. Added the authors' own conclusion; flagged the unverified vehicle split.

findings.claim: Taiwanese in-use scooters of Phases III and IV emitted 156% and 48% more CO, and 84% and 9% more HC, per unit fuel than Phase V; VOC per litre rose from 25.2 to 47.1 g/L between about 5,200 km and 47,600 km.
findings.value: Fuel economy 34.7 (V), 32.6 (IV), 29.5 (III) km/L. Phase V EF: CO 84.3, HC 29.4, NOx 8.0 g/L. Relative to V, III/IV: CO +156%/+48%, HC +84%/+9%, NOx -30%/-17%. VOC EF 25.2 +/- 8.0 g/L at 5,231 km vs 47.1 +/- 19.8 g/L at 47,617 km.
findings.setting: Taiwan; in-use four-stroke scooters; chassis dynamometer; fuel-based factors; 67 VOCs.
findings.citation: Tsai J-H, Yao Y-C, Huang P-H, Chiang H-L (2018). Fuel Economy and Volatile Organic Compound Exhaust Emission for Motorcycles with Various Running Mileages. Aerosol and Air Quality Research 18(12): 3056-3067.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex; authors via Crossref.
findings.quote: emission factors of a total of 67 volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were 25.2 ± 8.0 g L–1 for a running mileage of 5,231 ± 4,353 km, with emissions increasing to 47.1 ± 19.8 g L–1 for a running mileage of 47,617 ± 8,568 km
findings.caveats: Sample size not in abstract. Mileage and phase are confounded. Not idle-specific. The abstract's CO/HC percentages compare Phase III/IV with Phase V.
findings.useOnSite: Higher-mileage Taiwanese scooters emitted roughly twice the VOC per litre of fuel (47.1 vs 25.2 g/L).
findings.verifierNote: Numbers confirmed. Citation corrected to four authors (Chiang H-L added).

findings.claim: In a Taiwanese chassis-dynamometer test of nine four-stroke scooters (seven carburetted, two fuel-injected), cold-start driving gave 1.1-1.5 times the CO and 1.2-2.8 times the HC of hot-start driving; ratios were larger for 50 cc than 100/125 cc scooters; NOx differences were not pronounced.
findings.value: Cold/hot emission-factor ratio (g/km): CO 1.1-1.5; HC 1.2-2.8.
findings.setting: Taiwan; chassis dynamometer; cold- and hot-start cycles.
findings.citation: Yao Y-C, Tsai J-H, Ye H-F, Chiang H-L (2009). Comparison of Exhaust Emissions Resulting from Cold- and Hot-Start Motorcycle Driving Modes. J. Air & Waste Manage. Assoc. 59(11): 1339-1346.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex; bibliographic data via Crossref.
findings.quote: The ratio of emission factors (g/km) for cold- and hot-start driving cycles ranged from 1.1-1.5 (for CO) to 1.2-2.8 (for HCs).
findings.caveats: Nine vehicles, mostly carburetted. Whole-cycle ratios, not the first minutes at idle. The researcher's remark about fuel-injected ratios of 1.03-1.83 came from an unverified search summary and is WITHDRAWN. Abstract says warm-up may matter more for cars than for motorcycles.
findings.useOnSite: Cold-started scooters emitted up to about 1.5 times the CO and up to about 2.8 times the hydrocarbons of warmed-up ones over a test cycle (2009, mostly carburetted scooters).
findings.verifierNote: Numbers match; unverified fuel-injection ratio removed.

findings.claim: Inspection data from central Taiwan (1996-2002) showed two-stroke scooters emitted about ten times the HC of four-strokes at the idle test; failures were mainly CO-related; older and smaller-engine scooters failed more, but older scooters contributed little to total emissions because few remained.
findings.value: 2-stroke HC about 10x 4-stroke; failure rate due to CO nearly 4x that due to HC.
findings.setting: Central Air Quality Basin, Taiwan, I/M idle-test records 1996-2002.
findings.citation: Lin C-W, Lu S-J, Lin K-S (2006). Test emission characteristics of motorcycles in Central Taiwan. Science of the Total Environment 368(2-3): 435-443.
findings.design: Abstract read via Europe PMC; metadata via Crossref.
findings.quote: two-stroke motorcycles emitted approximately ten times greater HC than those of four-stroke motorcycles
findings.caveats: 1996-2002 data, mostly pre-catalyst fleet. The abstract states that older motorcycles do not contribute significantly to total emissions because they are few, so this paper does not support a claim that old scooters dominate fleet emissions.
findings.useOnSite: At the idle test, two-stroke scooters of the late 1990s emitted about ten times the HC of four-strokes.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches.

findings.claim: Taipei inspection data 1996-2005 show failure rates rising for scooters older than 3 years or beyond 10,000 km, with two-strokes failing more.
findings.value: Testing rate about 50% -> 70%; failure rate about 15% -> 10%; failure rates rise beyond 3 years or 10,000 km.
findings.setting: Taipei City, idle-test data 1996-2005.
findings.citation: Chen Y-C, Chen L-Y, Jeng F-T (2009). Analysis of Motorcycle Exhaust Regular Testing Data - A Case Study of Taipei City. J. Air & Waste Manage. Assoc. 59(6): 757-762.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex; authors via Crossref.
findings.quote: failure rates show a gradually increasing trend for motorcycles older than 3 yr or used for mileages greater than 10,000 km
findings.caveats: Data end in 2005, before the 2007 phase 5 standard. Idle-test performance only.
findings.useOnSite: Taipei's inspection records (1996-2005) show failures climbing after about 3 years or 10,000 km.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches.

findings.claim: One Taiwanese four-stroke motorcycle emitted about 2.07 x 10^4 particles/cm3 at idle, slightly LESS than at 15 km/h (2.35 x 10^4) and 30 km/h (2.60 x 10^4).
findings.value: Total number concentration: idle 2.07e4; 15 km/h 2.35e4; 30 km/h 2.60e4 #/cm3.
findings.setting: Taiwan; four-stroke motorcycle (4-st/mc), 95-octane unleaded gasoline; idle, 15, 30 km/h; PAH analysis.
findings.citation: Chien S-M, Huang Y-J (2010). Sizes and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon composition distributions of nano, ultrafine, fine, and coarse particulates emitted from a four-stroke motorcycle. J. Environ. Sci. Health A 45(13): 1768-1774.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex and Europe PMC.
findings.quote: The particle total number concentrations (TNCs) emitted while idling and at 15 and 30 km/h were 2.07 x 10⁴, 2.35 x 10⁴, and 2.60 x 10⁴ #/cm³, respectively; i.e., they increased at elevated speeds.
findings.caveats: Concentration in a diluted sample, not an emission factor. The abstract (whose first sentence is truncated in the databases) does not state the number of vehicles; 'single motorcycle' is inferred from the title. Strongest PAH-related carcinogenic potency was at 30 km/h; idle PAHs were lower-molecular-weight, suspected from unburned fuel.
findings.useOnSite: Do not claim idling emits more particles than driving; the only Taiwanese idle particle-number datum rises slightly with speed.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers match; 'single vehicle' downgraded to inferred.

findings.claim: Five common Hanoi motorcycle models emitted on average 60.9 g/h CO, 10.3 g/h HC, 1.8 g/h NOx and 534.3 g/h CO2 at idle, burning about 180 g of fuel per hour; idling made up 2.23% of fleet CO, 1.14% of HC and 1.03% of NOx in Hanoi.
findings.value: Steady idle: CO 60.9, HC 10.3, NOx 1.8, CO2 534.3 g/h; fuel about 180 g/h. Fleet idle share (3.9 million motorcycles, 2018): CO 2.23%, CO2 3.19%, HC 1.14%, NOx 1.03%.
findings.setting: Hanoi, Vietnam; laboratory; five models commonly used in Hanoi.
findings.citation: Nguyen Y-L T, Le A T, Nguyen Duc K, Duy, Nguyen (2021; five authors per Crossref). A study on emission and fuel consumption of motorcycles in idle mode and the impacts on air quality in Hanoi, Vietnam. Int. J. Urban Sciences 25(4): 522-541.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex; Crossref lists five authors (Nguyen, Le, Duc, Duy, Nguyen).
findings.quote: The average idling emissions of pollutants CO, CO2, HC and NOx were 60.9, 534.3, 10.3 and 1.8 g/h, respectively.
findings.caveats: Not Taiwanese; standard, mileage and fuel-injection status not in the abstract. Idle is a small share of fleet totals in Hanoi, so do not say idling dominates overall; its importance is spatial concentration at intersections. 60.9 g/h is about 0.017 g/s.
findings.useOnSite: Laboratory tests of common Vietnamese scooters measured about 61 g of CO per hour at idle (not Taiwanese data).
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches; truncated author placeholders kept because only family names were checked.

findings.claim: In a Vietnamese test of 15 motorcycles, restarting used about 0.069 g of fuel, so switching off is recommended if stopped more than 14 s.
findings.value: Idle fuel 0.141 g (5 s), 0.703 g (30 s); restart 0.069 +/- 0.0007 g/start; break-even 14 s; restart fuel 90.5% less than 30 s idle; efficiency gain at least 38.1%.
findings.setting: Vietnam; 15 motorcycles aged 0-15 years, fuel-injected and carburetted; controlled conditions.
findings.citation: Nguyen Y-L T, Than Thi H Y, Nguyen Duc K, Le A T, et al. (2025). Analyzing fuel consumption characteristics of idle and re-start options for motorcycles at intersections in Vietnam. J. Chinese Inst. Engineers 49(1): 112-127.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex; authors via Crossref.
findings.quote: If stopped for more than 14 s, turning off the MC engine is recommended to reduce fuel waste and minimize wear on engine components.
findings.caveats: Fuel only; pollutant emissions at restart are not reported in the abstract.
findings.useOnSite: Fuel-wise, switching off at a red light longer than about 14 s saves fuel (Vietnamese test).
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches.

findings.claim: A chassis-dynamometer study of two market idle-stop motorcycles found that restart emissions outweighed the savings from engine shut-off; an older test cited in the abstract showed up to 55% more exhaust with idle-stop on; ECU recalibration was judged feasible.
findings.value: Cumulative increase in emissions in the restart phase > decrease in the shut-off phase; abstract states 'even a 175 percent of emissions reduction could be achieved'.
findings.setting: Two market idle-stop motorcycle types; chassis dynamometer; six driving cycles; idle-stop on vs off. Authors affiliated with the Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) per Crossref.
findings.citation: Chen C-L, Lin Z-D (2013). Feasibility Study of Emission Improvement through Transient Emission Characteristics Analysis for Idle-Stop Motorcycles. SAE Technical Paper 2013-32-9052.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex; authors and affiliation via Crossref.
findings.quote: the cumulative value of increased exhaust emissions during restart phase after engine shut off was higher than the cumulative value of decreased exhaust emissions during engine shut off phase
findings.caveats: Abstract only; pollutants not itemised; the 55% is attributed to 'some test data', not this study; '175 percent' is as printed and cannot literally exceed 100%. The market of the tested models (Taiwan or elsewhere) is not stated in the abstract. 2013 vehicles.
findings.useOnSite: An early idle-stop study showed restart emissions can cancel out shut-off savings; air-pollutant benefit depends on calibration.
findings.verifierNote: Affiliation corrected from ARTC to ITRI (Crossref); 'Taiwan-specific' downgraded to partly because the abstract does not name where the tested vehicles were sold.

findings.claim: A 125 cc Euro 4 scooter in congested Poznan traffic emitted 57% more CO and 4% more HC, 10% less NOx and about 12% less fuel/CO2 with start-stop enabled.
findings.value: CO +57%, HC +4%, NOx -10%, fuel/CO2 about -12%.
findings.setting: Poznan, Poland; one 125 cc scooter; real-world measurement over 7.35 km.
findings.citation: Lijewski P, Szymlet N, Fuc P, Domowicz A, Rymaniak L (2021). The effect of start-stop systems on scooter exhaust emissions. Transportation Research Part D 91: 102684.
findings.design: Abstract read via Semantic Scholar API; authors via Crossref.
findings.quote: the actual emissions of CO and HC were greater by 57% and 4%, respectively for the scooter with the start-stop system enabled, while the emission of NOx decreased by 10%
findings.caveats: Single scooter, European, Euro 4.
findings.useOnSite: One European test found start-stop saved fuel but raised CO and HC; evidence on tailpipe benefit is mixed.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches.

findings.claim: A 2026 study (Dhital, Yang, et al.) evaluates real-world tailpipe benefits of motorcycle idle-stop systems; results not accessible.
findings.value: n/a
findings.setting: Not verified (not known to be Taiwanese data).
findings.citation: Dhital N B, Yang H-H, Hsieh T-J, Chen H-W, Huang S-W (2026). Effectiveness of Motorcycle Idle-Stop Systems in Mitigating Real-World Tailpipe Emissions of Air Pollutants. Emission Control Science and Technology 12(1): 5.
findings.design: Existence, authors, journal, volume/article number and date (18 Mar 2026) confirmed via Crossref; abstract withheld by Crossref and Semantic Scholar.
findings.caveats: Results unknown; do not cite any number.
findings.useOnSite: Do not cite until abstract or full text is read.
findings.verifierNote: Citation exists; content could not be opened.

findings.claim: Taiwan's emission standard requires manufacturers with prior-year domestic sales of 10,000+ motorcycles to make at least 20% (from 2017) and 50% (from 2021) of their engine families idle-stop, hybrid or electric.
findings.value: 20% of engine families from 1 Jan 2017; 50% from 1 Jan 2021 (electric models counted by model).
findings.setting: Taiwan; new motorcycle approval, phases 6 and 7.
findings.citation: Ministry of Environment (Taiwan) / Executive Yuan Gazette vol. 29 no. 121 (30 June 2023), Standards for Air Pollutant Emissions from Mobile Sources (移動污染源空氣污染物排放標準), Article 6 notes (六); ARTC article https://www.artc.org.tw/tw/knowledge/articles/2617.
findings.design: Gazette note text read by verifier; ARTC article (written about 2014) describes the same rule as 停等零污染.
findings.quote: 上年度全年新車國內銷售量達一萬輛以上之製造廠或進口商，當年度須生產或進口惰轉熄火(idle-stop)功能機車或複合動力電動機車或電動機車 ... 達該廠商當年度機車內銷總引擎族數量之50%以上
findings.caveats: Counts engine families, not scooters sold or on the road; no official count of idle-stop scooters found. Riders can usually override idle-stop. Pre-2017 scooters have none.
findings.useOnSite: Since 2021 at least half of each large maker's engine families must be idle-stop, hybrid or electric; this is not half of scooters on the road.
findings.verifierNote: Gazette and ARTC both say this.

findings.claim: A Taiwanese stated-preference survey estimated motorcyclists' willingness to turn off the engine at red lights at 82 s on average (101 s if legislated), with projected savings of 1021 L gasoline and 0.56 t CO2 per hour at the studied intersection in peak periods.
findings.value: WTO 82 s (Spike model); 101 s (if legislated); 1021 L/h and 0.56 t CO2/h.
findings.setting: Urban intersections in Taiwan; the abstract says the government introduced an idling-stop policy in early 2007.
findings.citation: Jou R-C, Wu Y-C, Chen K-H (2011). Analysis of the environmental benefits of a motorcycle idling stop policy at urban intersections. Transportation 38(6): 1017-1033.
findings.design: Verifier read the full abstract on the IAOR/IFORS database record (publisher abstract not retrievable).
findings.quote: Results obtained from the Spike model showed that the average motorcyclist’s WTO is 82 s.
findings.caveats: Stated preference, not measured. 1021 L of gasoline (about 2.3 t CO2) and 0.56 t CO2 are mutually inconsistent as printed; do not reuse either.
findings.useOnSite: Taiwanese riders said they would switch off for about 82 s on average; about willingness, not measured emissions.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract text seen; numbers match; adds the 2007 policy context.

findings.claim: A Thai on-road study of 30 riders on a congested signalised corridor found idle-time proportion significantly influenced fuel use and emissions, whereas aggressive acceleration/deceleration did not.
findings.value: Qualitative.
findings.setting: Khon Kaen, Thailand; instrumented motorcycle; morning peak.
findings.citation: Seedam A, Satiennam T, Radpukdee T, Satiennam W, Ratanavaraha V (2017). Motorcycle On-Road Driving Parameters Influencing Fuel Consumption and Emissions on Congested Signalized Urban Corridor. J. Advanced Transportation 2017: 5859789.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex; authors via Crossref (five authors).
findings.quote: proportion of idle time significantly influenced fuel consumption and emissions of motorcycle driving on a congested signalized urban corridor, though aggressive driving behavior, hard acceleration and deceleration, did not have the same kind of influence
findings.caveats: No numbers in abstract; one test motorcycle; trip-level effect, not an instantaneous pull-away spike. No measured pull-away spike was found by researcher or verifier.
findings.useOnSite: On-road evidence says idle time drives trip fuel use and emissions more than hard acceleration.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches; citation completed to five authors.

findings.claim: Taiwan's inventory work ranks motorcycle HC and benzene emission factors above gasoline cars, but PM2.5 and NOx below gasoline and diesel vehicles.
findings.value: Activity 2021: gasoline passenger cars 42.6% of road vehicle-km, four-stroke motorcycles 32.6%. Order: PM2.5 and NOx diesel > gasoline > motorcycle; HC motorcycle > gasoline; benzene motorcycle > gasoline >= diesel; formaldehyde diesel > motorcycle >= gasoline.
findings.setting: Taiwan 2013-2021 inventory; models MOVES, MOBILE6.2 and dynamometer data; fleet averages.
findings.citation: Tsai J-H, Chen J-Y, Chiang H-L (2023). Airborne Air Pollutant Emission Characteristics of Mobile Vehicles in Taiwan. Atmosphere 14(6): 916.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex.
findings.quote: the HC emission factor was compiled with the use of gasoline vehicle dynamometer data, and the results showed that motorcycle > gasoline vehicles
findings.caveats: Modelled fleet-average per-km factors; not idle; numbers not in abstract. Do not say scooters out-emit cars on PM2.5 or NOx.
findings.useOnSite: Per km, scooters emit more unburned hydrocarbons and benzene than gasoline cars but less PM2.5 and NOx.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches.

findings.claim: A Taipei tunnel study found heavy-duty vehicles dominated PM2.5 and eBC, while light-duty vehicles and motorcycles influenced CO and CO2; the tunnel CO emission factor was higher than earlier studies, attributed to a larger motorcycle fraction.
findings.value: No numbers in abstract.
findings.setting: Urban tunnel in Taipei, real driving; regression by vehicle class.
findings.citation: Ting Y-C, Chang P-K, Hung P-C, Chou C C-K, Chi K-H, Hsiao T-C (2023). Characterizing emission factors and oxidative potential of motorcycle emissions in a real-world tunnel environment. Environmental Research 234: 116601.
findings.design: Abstract read via Europe PMC (the verifier read it).
findings.quote: The CO emission factor for transportation inside the tunnel was found to be higher than those in previous studies, likely owing to the increased fraction of MCs, which generally emit higher CO levels.
findings.caveats: Steady-flow tunnel driving, not idling. The attribution of higher CO to motorcycles is the authors' inference ('likely'). Full-text factors not read.
findings.useOnSite: Taipei tunnel measurements link scooters to high CO, while PM2.5 came mainly from heavy-duty vehicles.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches.

findings.claim: A roadside remote-sensing study in middle Taiwan found older vehicles are higher emitters and contribute significantly more to fleet emissions; it covers vehicles in general and does not mention motorcycles in the abstract.
findings.value: No numbers in abstract.
findings.setting: Middle Taiwan; remote sensing of large fleets.
findings.citation: Ko Y-W, Cho C-H (2006). Characterization of large fleets of vehicle exhaust emissions in middle Taiwan by remote sensing. Science of the Total Environment 354: 75-82.
findings.design: Abstract read via Europe PMC; Crossref lookup failed so volume and pages (354, 75-82) are as given by the original and not independently checked.
findings.quote: It indicates those relatively older vehicles are higher emitters and contribute significantly more to total fleet emissions.
findings.caveats: Not scooter-specific; old; cannot support any 'dirtiest 10-20% of scooters' claim.
findings.useOnSite: Do not use for scooters.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches; volume/pages unverified.

findings.claim: Two-stroke scooters (non-Taiwanese study) can have organic aerosol and aromatic emission factors up to thousands of times those of other vehicle classes, and their exhaust forms secondary organic aerosol and reactive oxygen species.
findings.value: Up to 'thousands of times higher'.
findings.setting: Laboratory two-stroke scooter tests (location not stated in abstract; first-hand knowledge: Europe) with ambient context.
findings.citation: Platt S M, El Haddad I, Pieber S M, et al. (2014). Two-stroke scooters are a dominant source of air pollution in many cities. Nature Communications 5: 3749.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex; metadata via Crossref.
findings.quote: vehicles that constitute a small fraction of the fleet, but can dominate urban vehicular pollution through organic aerosol and aromatic emission factors up to thousands of times higher than from other vehicle classes
findings.caveats: Two-stroke only. The claim that Taiwan had already phased out new two-stroke sales was not verified; the MOENV table shows 243,725 pre-2004 two-strokes notified in 2025 versus 9.88 million four-strokes. Not an idle measurement.
findings.useOnSite: Non-Taiwanese: a few old two-stroke scooters can produce disproportionate organic particle pollution.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches; unverified phase-out sentence flagged.

findings.claim: Four large in-use motorcycles (599-1078 cc) emitted 26-270 billion non-volatile particles/km, 29-75% of particles (5-560 nm) were below 23 nm, NH3 27-273 mg/km tied to fuel-rich transients.
findings.value: Particles 2.6e10-2.7e11 /km; 29-75% under 23 nm; NH3 27-273 mg/km; NO 30-509 mg/km.
findings.setting: Czech Republic; four large motorcycles 2008-2015; WMTC cold and hot start; chassis dynamometer.
findings.citation: Pechout M, Jindra P, Hart J, Vojtisek-Lom M (2022). Regulated and unregulated emissions and exhaust flow measurement of four in-use high performance motorcycles. Atmospheric Environment: X 14: 100170.
findings.design: Abstract read via OpenAlex; authors via Crossref (four authors).
findings.quote: The average number of non-volatile particles per km varied from 26 to 270 billion (2.6–27 × 1011).
findings.caveats: Large motorcycles, not scooters; not Asian; no idle breakdown. Mechanism only.
findings.useOnSite: Mechanism only: motorcycles emit very small particles; label as large European motorcycles.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches, incl. 29-75% under 23 nm.

findings.claim: Taiwan limits evaporative HC from new scooters to 2 g per test (1991), 2000 mg (2017) and 1500 mg (2021, SHED); crankcase vapour must not be vented to atmosphere (1988); an onboard refuelling vapour recovery system for scooters was prototyped in Taiwan.
findings.value: Evaporative HC per test: 2 g from 1 Jul 1991; 2000 mg from 1 Jan 2017; 1500 mg from 1 Jan 2021; crankcase blow-by not to be emitted from 1 Jan 1988.
findings.setting: Taiwan type approval; SHED from 2017.
findings.citation: Ministry of Environment (Taiwan) / Executive Yuan Gazette vol. 29 no. 121 (30 June 2023), Standards for Air Pollutant Emissions from Mobile Sources (移動污染源空氣污染物排放標準), Article 7; Wu, Chung, Lin, Lin (2019). Evaluation of Evaporative Emission and Feasibility of an Onboard Refueling Vapor Recovery System for Scooters. Energies 12(4): 704.
findings.design: Article 7 table read by verifier; Wu et al. abstract read via OpenAlex; authors via Crossref.
findings.quote: 每次測試2000毫克 ... 每次測試1500毫克; 'A significant improvement on the leaking problem of fuel vapor is gained by using the proposed ORVR system'
findings.caveats: Type-approval limits only; no in-use evaporative measurement found. The statement that scooters have no refuelling-vapour control is an inference from Article 7 (which regulates tank/fuel-system evaporation only) and from Wu et al. describing ORVR as a prospect.
findings.useOnSite: New scooters are limited to 1.5 g of evaporative HC per test since 2021.
findings.verifierNote: Limits and dates match the gazette.

findings.claim: Taiwan's phase 5 motorcycle standard (July 2007) is equivalent to Euro 3; phases 6 and 7 (2017, 2021) are equivalent to Euro 4 and Euro 5 delayed by a year, with the test cycle changing from six ECE urban cycles plus one EUDC to WMTC.
findings.value: Phase 5 = Euro 3-equivalent (Jul 2007); phase 6 = 2017; phase 7 = 2021; NMHC and PM (direct-injection only) added from phase 7.
findings.setting: Taiwan; ARTC explainer written about 2014.
findings.citation: Automotive Research and Testing Center (ARTC), 機車第六期及第七期污染排放標準將於2017年及2021年實施.
findings.design: Verifier fetched and read the article.
findings.quote: 台灣機車第五期污染排放標準等同於歐三(Euro 3)的排放標準，未來制定的第六期及第七期亦等同於歐四及歐五排放標準，並延後歐盟一年實施
findings.caveats: Phase numbers 1-4 (1988, 1991, 1998, 2004) are not stated in this source; they are inferred from Tsai et al. grouping (Phases III, IV, V) and remain unverified. The article is a pre-2017 forward-looking explainer.
findings.useOnSite: Use to explain why g/km limits across 2004 and 2017+ are not directly comparable.
findings.verifierNote: Added to support the phase labelling and the test-cycle caveat.

doNotClaim: Do not say idling scooters emit MORE particles than moving scooters: the one Taiwanese idle datum (Chien & Huang 2010) has idle number concentration slightly lower than at 15 and 30 km/h.
Do not say scooters emit more PM2.5 or NOx than cars; Tsai et al. 2023 rank them lowest for both. Their per-km disadvantage is CO, HC and benzene.
Do not give a pull-away spike factor; no scooter study quantifying it was found. The only on-road evidence (Thailand) found idle time, not hard acceleration, mattered.
Do not state the share of emissions from the dirtiest 10-20% of scooters; no Taiwanese scooter data were found. Ko & Cho 2006 is about vehicles in general; Lin 2006 found old scooters few.

Do not say idle-stop is widespread on the road or that it cuts pollutants; the mandate counts engine families, and measured effects are mixed (CO +57%, HC +4%, fuel -12% in Poland; restart emissions can outweigh savings in an ITRI study).
Do not say '96% of scooters are clean': 3.78-3.93% is the failure rate among inspected scooters at a lenient idle test; non-attenders are untested.
Do not compare CO limits of 7.0 (2004) and 1.0 (2021) g/km, or 3.5 (1998) and 7.0 (2004), as like for like: the test cycle changed (ECE-type to WMTC per ARTC).
Do not quote HC+NOx as 3.75-4.5 g/km for 1988-2003: the actual new-type HC+NOx limits were 4.4/5.5 (1988), 2.4/3.0 (1991), 1.75/2.0 (1998-2003).
Do not say the age trend is monotonic or that 16-year-old scooters fail at 5%: age 16 is 3.57%; the rise starts at 17.
Do not attribute Hanoi idle rates (60.9 g/h CO) to Taiwanese scooters.
Do not reuse Jou et al. 2011's 1021 L and 0.56 t CO2 figures; they are projections from stated preferences and inconsistent with each other.
Do not cite any result from Dhital et al. 2026 until its abstract or full text is read.
Do not describe the Chen & Lin 2013 SAE authors as ARTC staff; Crossref lists ITRI.
gaps: No Taiwanese per-scooter idle emission rate (g/h or g/min) for CO, HC, NOx; the only idle rates are Hanoi laboratory data. No per-vehicle comparison of idling scooter versus idling passenger car.
No Taiwanese scooter PM mass, particle number or ultrafine factors by mode with modern fuel-injected scooters; Chien & Huang 2010 is the only idle particle datum.
No quantitative green-light pull-away spike for scooters.
No Taiwanese scooter remote-sensing study and so no high-emitter share.

Registered scooter counts by emission phase were not found; MOENV age tables are only a proxy (about 1.02 million inspected scooters aged 20+ in 2025). Phase numbering 1-4 (1988, 1991, 1998, 2004) is unverified; only phase 5-7 are confirmed (ARTC).
No official count of idle-stop scooters in the fleet; Dhital et al. 2026 abstract unreachable.
No in-use evaporative or refuelling VOC measurements for Taiwanese scooters.
Full texts of the AAQR, JAWMA and Results in Engineering papers were not opened (publishers blocked); only abstracts. Ko & Cho 2006 volume/pages not independently verified.
Pedestrian exposure or health effects at a crossing are outside this scope and not covered by any study here.
